name: Starter: Norwegian
about: Norwegian (Bokmål) word order in real, everyday sentences.

words.komme: to come (kommer til å: to be going to)
words.form: condition (i form: in shape, feeling well)
words.stå: to stand, to be (of upright things)

hvordan-har-du-det.about: A greeting you learn whole: literally, how have you it? Answer with Bra, takk (fine, thanks).

hva-heter-du.about: Literally, what are you called? Answer with Jeg heter and your name.

unnskyld.about: To get someone's attention, or to say sorry.

det-er.about: Also it is: Det er kaffe på kjøkkenet (there's coffee in the kitchen); Det er kaldt (it's cold).

er-du-snill.about: A friendly please after a request: literally, are you kind.

takk-for-maten.about: Said to whoever made the food, as you get up from the table.

concept.line: The present is the same for every person and usually ends in -r (jeg jobber, hun jobber); it means both I work and I'm working.
In a main-clause statement the verb that shows the tense comes second (not always the second word): when a time, a place or a whole clause comes first, the subject follows that verb.

My, your and our match the noun and usually come after it, with the noun in its definite form (bilen min, huset mitt, nøklene mine); in front of a plain noun they add emphasis or sound more formal (min bror).
In a yes/no question the verb that shows the tense comes first; after a question word it comes before the subject (unless the question word is the subject).
Every noun is masculine (en), feminine (ei, or en) or neuter (et), and the words with it match: en stor bil, et stort kjøkken.
With a noun on its own, the is an ending: bil, bilen (the car); hus, huset (the house); jente, jenta (the girl).
